title: 98 doors open. Stay or switch?
hook: Two doors left looks like 50/50. With 100 doors to start, does it still?

knows: probability as a fraction of equally likely cases
the rules of a game-show door pick

misconception: Once only two doors are left, each is equally likely to hide the car, so switching changes nothing.
objective: The learner can explain that the first pick keeps its 1-in-N chance because the host can always open empty doors, so the one door the knowing host leaves shut carries the remaining (N-1)/N.

claims.text: With 100 doors, one car, and a host who knows where the car is and always opens 98 empty doors other than yours, switching wins with probability 99/100 and staying with 1/100.
claims.source: Staying wins only if the first pick was the car: 1/100. The host never opens the car, so whenever the first pick is empty (99/100) the door he leaves shut is the car. Switching wins exactly when staying loses: 99/100.

claims.text: With 3 doors and the same knowing host, switching wins 2 times in 3.
claims.source: Same argument with N = 3: stay wins 1/3, switch wins (N-1)/N = 2/3.

claims.text: The host can always open 98 empty doors whatever you picked, so his opening does not change the 1-in-100 chance of your first pick.
claims.source: Of the 99 doors you did not pick, at least 98 are empty, so the host's action is possible in every case and P(your door has the car | host opens 98 empty doors) = P(your door has the car) = 1/100.

claims.text: If the host opened 98 of the other doors at random and they happened to be empty, your door and the remaining door would each have a 50% chance.
claims.source: Bayes: P(mine | 98 random openings all empty) = (1/100 x 1) / (1/100 x 1 + 99/100 x 1/99) = 1/2. P(all 98 empty | car elsewhere) = 1/99, the chance his random choice spares the car's door.

claims.text: The stage's rounds use a seeded generator with the car equally likely behind every door; 'Play 100 rounds' plays each round with a random first pick and counts how staying and switching would have done; 'Guessing host: 1,000 rounds' has a host who opens doors at random, throws away rounds where he hit the car, and over many batches staying and switching each win about half of the kept rounds.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/monty-hall-100-doors/model.ts (carFor, hostLeaves, batch, guessingBatch). Earlier re-run with node --experimental-strip-types: first batch at 100 doors stay 2, switch 98; at 10 doors 7/93; at 3 doors 30/70. Over 100 batches of 100: 100 doors 92/9,908; 10 doors 1,002/8,998; 3 doors 3,303/6,697. In every round exactly one of stay or switch wins. guessingBatch (builder re-run 2026-10-13): first 1,000 guessing rounds kept 14 at 100 doors (stay 6, switch 8), 209 at 10 doors (107/102), 671 at 3 doors (353/318); over 200 batches of 1,000: 100 doors kept 4,037 (stay 2,017, switch 2,020), 10 doors kept 39,759 (19,868/19,891), 3 doors kept 132,924 (66,100/66,824). Kept share per round: 1/N + (N-1)/N x 1/(N-1) = 2/N. recall.question: Ten doors, one car. You pick one; a host who knows where the car is opens eight empty doors. Should you switch to the last closed door?
options: No: your first pick is safer
recall.why: Your pick was a 1-in-10 guess and the host's openings cannot change that. The other 9 in 10 all land on the one door he chose to leave shut.
